drills.q: Explain precisely why parameterized queries are a complete fix for SQL injection while escaping is not.
drills.a: Parameterization compiles the query structure before any user data enters, binding values through a separate channel never re-interpreted as syntax -- no code path lets a bound value alter structure. Escaping neutralizes dangerous characters within the SAME channel as syntax, only as complete as the escaping function's coverage of every syntactically significant sequence -- real gaps exist historically (e.g. MySQL multi-byte charset bypasses of naive backslash-escaping).

drills.q: Is there a performance cost to parameterization that would justify escaping instead?
drills.a: No -- prepared statement query plans are frequently cached and reused, often making parameterized queries FASTER under repeated load than re-parsing a novel concatenated string each time. No legitimate performance tradeoff favors escaping.

drills.q: Walk through extracting a password hash character by character via boolean-blind SQL injection, and give the actual request count.
drills.a: Inject a condition like ASCII(SUBSTRING(password,N,1)) > X per position, observing which of two distinguishable behaviors results; binary-search X over the printable ASCII range (~95 values, ceil(log2(95)) ~ 7 requests/char). A 32-character hash takes ~224 requests total -- what sqlmap automates.

drills.q: What if an app gives no distinguishable true/false behavior at all for boolean-blind injection?
drills.a: Fall back to time-blind injection (IF(condition, SLEEP(5), SLEEP(0))), inferring truth from response latency instead of content -- much slower since you wait out a real delay per query. If even timing is unusable, out-of-band exfiltration via DNS/HTTP callouts is the remaining channel.

drills.q: What makes second-order SQL injection uniquely difficult to catch via code review, compared to first-order injection?
drills.a: The payload is stored via a correctly parameterized write -- genuinely no injection at that point -- and only becomes exploitable when a DIFFERENT code path reads the value back and builds a different, often unparameterized query, since the developer there assumed already-stored data was safe. Reviewing the write path in isolation finds nothing wrong.

drills.q: How would you actually find a second-order injection in a real codebase audit?
drills.a: Trace every value that ends up in a query string back to its origin, treating 'this came from our own database' as irrelevant to trust level. The correct question is never 'where did this data come from' but 'is THIS specific query, right here, parameterized' -- applied uniformly regardless of upstream validation elsewhere.

drills.q: A codebase uses an ORM exclusively and a security review still finds SQL injection. Where is it most likely, and why?
drills.a: Almost certainly a raw-SQL escape hatch (.raw()/.extra()/text()/find_by_sql with concatenated user input) or dynamic identifier construction (sort column/table name from user input) -- parameterization binds values, never identifiers, so even fully ORM-based code can have this gap.

drills.q: Design a defense for a feature supporting user-selectable ORDER BY columns without introducing SQL injection.
drills.a: Parameterization doesn't apply to identifiers at all. Use an explicit allowlist mapping user input against a small, fixed set of known-valid column names/directions server-side, rejecting anything not matching exactly, and only interpolate the validated, allowlisted identifier -- never the raw user string.

drills.q: Explain the NoSQL operator-injection authentication bypass and why 'MongoDB doesn't use SQL strings' doesn't make it immune to injection.
drills.a: If a client-supplied value is passed directly into a query position, sending {"password": {"$ne": null}} makes MongoDB interpret $ne as an operator (not-equal-to-null), true for nearly any account -- bypassing auth with zero guessing. Not string concatenation, but the identical structural bug: untrusted input interpreted as control (an operator) rather than a plain value.

drills.q: What is the structural reason prompt injection has no fix analogous to parameterized queries?
drills.a: SQL has a formal grammar letting a parser mechanically enforce 'this slot is a bound value, never re-parsed as a keyword.' Natural language has no equivalent grammar -- no token reliably marks 'data, not instruction,' and the model is trained specifically to find and follow instructions wherever they appear, since instructions and data share one undifferentiated channel.

drills.q: An LLM agent has tool access to send emails and query a customer database. Design a mitigation strategy assuming prompt injection cannot be fully prevented.
drills.a: Assume any processed content could contain an injected instruction; design tools so a successful injection can't cause serious harm -- scope the database tool to read-only on non-sensitive tables, gate email-sending behind human confirmation for anything beyond a pre-approved template. This is privilege separation/least-privilege authorization applied to agent tool access: the goal isn't preventing manipulation, it's making manipulation not matter.

drills.q: A startup claims their 'AI firewall' fully prevents prompt injection. How do you evaluate that claim, using the SQL-injection lens?
drills.a: Ask whether the defense is structural/deterministic (like parameterization -- architecturally impossible regardless of input) or probabilistic pattern-detection (like a blocklist/WAF -- catches known patterns, misses novel ones by construction). Since no known architecture provides structural instruction/data separation for natural language, any 'fully prevents' claim is almost certainly the second category with a real false-negative rate -- request actual red-team results, not marketing language.
